newsitem.title: USA: Penney's Eckerd buy sign of diversification trend.
newsitem.headline: Penney's Eckerd buy sign of diversification trend.

text.p: J.C. Penney Co.'s agreement to buy drugstore chain Eckerd Corp. shows retailers again are diversifying in order to grow, but the risks are lower now than during the buying binges of the past.

Penney, the nation's fifth-largest retailer, announced Sunday it would acquire Eckerd in a deal valued at about $3.2 billion. After the deal, Penney's Thrift drugstores would be third-largest in the nation.

Dallas-based Penney has swallowed two other drugstore chains and a big piece of a third during the past 18 months. The deals come as expansion among department stores has slowed to a trickle, forcing Penney and other mainline retailers to diversify to grow.

"(Penney) has some real tough competitive issues in their core business," said Michael Exstein of PaineWebber. "The issue for them is how do they harness their financial resources to offset an intense business (environment)."
While Penney has been in the drugstore business for a quarter century, the company only recently turned to that sector to boost stagnant revenunes and lift profits.

Like Penney, other retail giants such as Sears, Roebuck and Co. and Limited Inc. have bought or launched new retail formats to overcome sluggishness in their mature businesses. But unlike the buying boom that damaged many chains earlier this decade, they have not strayed as far from core operations.

"They're sticking much closer to retailing than in the past," said William Wetreich, managing director of corporate ratings at Standard & Poor's. "But you could also point to as many that are refocusing rather than diversifying."
S&P on Monday put Penney on its watch list with negative implicatons and placed Eckerd on watch with a positive outlook.

Under the deal, Penney would offer $35 a share for about half of Eckerd's shares. In a second stage, Eckerd holders would receive 0.6604 Penney share for each Eckerd share, and Penney would assume $760 million in Eckerd debt, putting the value of the deal at about $3.2 billion.
Penney's shares fell $1.875 to $51.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
The deal is expected to dilute Penney's earnings in 1997 but add to profits the next year. It would also raise Penney's debt-to-capital ratio to an estimated 60 percent from 43 percent, S&P said.

Most Wall Street analysts praised the deal, which is expected to produce cost savings of about $100 million by 1998 and give Penney a bigger presence in drug retailing, which is growing faster than department stores.

"Department store retailers have two choices, either consolidation or diversification," said Eileen Leary, a vice president at State Street Research. "Retailers need to look to other avenues for growth."
Sears, for example, is moving outside traditional shopping malls for growth.

Sears, the nation's third-largest retailer, spent most of this decade shedding financial businesses such as Allstate Corp. and Dean Witter, Discover & Co. But its growth plans call for it to rely less on its big mall-based operation and more on free-standing stores such as Sears Hardware.

Earlier this year, Sears bought Orchard Supply Hardware Stores Corp. for about $415 million to fold into the hardware business and is searching for more acquisitions. Its strategy calls for more acquisitions, but Sears does not plan to stray from the retailing or into totally new store formats like bookstores.
Penney's biggest challenge is to prove its drug store deals will benefit the bottomline, analysts said.

The Eckerd deal, which still requires the approval of Eckerd's shareholders, still could fall apart if another bidder emerged. But most other big drugstore chains are busy gobbling up competitors or unable to top Penney's price.
Penney is paying about 63 percent of Eckerd's revenues and $1.9 million per location, a bit more than some recent deals, analysts said.
"The Eckerd name and franchise in the South is very valuable," said Jack Russo of A.G. Edwards. "It's full of opportunity. The price theoretically could go higher."

Melville Corp.'s CVS drug stores last month opened nine stores in Atlanta where Eckerd is the market leader. CVS officials could not be reached for comment on whether the company is mulling a competing bid for Eckerd.
Since Eckerd's President and Chief Executive Frank Newman will become chief executive of the Thrift and Eckerd business, Eckerd's management may not be receptive to another offer, analysts said.
